D'où il s'ensuit que le droit à la présomption d'innocence tel que défini à l'article 7 (1) (b) a été violé. Sur la violation du droit d'être jugé dans un délai raisonnable par une juridiction impartiale

La Commission relève que l'expression « délai raisonnable » comprend une juxtaposition de deux termes : Celui de « délai » et celui de « raisonnable ». Le premier se réfère à un intervalle de temps pendant lequel s'accomplit une action ; et dans le cadre d'une instance judiciaire, un intervalle de temps dans lequel se produit un jugement. Quant à l'adjectif « raisonnable », il peut être défini comme étant ce qui est logique et satisfaisant. Ainsi, dans le contexte de la Charte africaine, l'expression « délai raisonnable » signifierait un intervalle de temps qui n'est ni étonnamment long, ni abusivement court. En d'autres termes, la Charte veut que le procès soit d'une durée acceptable ou qui n'est pas excessivement longue.

Ainsi comprise, il reste pour la Commission à déterminer la durée d'un délai raisonnable. Ni la Charte, ni d'autres instruments internationaux de protection des droits de l'homme n'en donnent la durée exacte et maximum. Cependant, dans l'affaire Article 19 c./ Erythrée, la Commission a indiqué que la question liée à ce qui est raisonnable ne peut pas être exprimé en termes de délai global qui s'applique à tous les cas, mais elle doit plutôt dépendre des circonstances. Elle s'est ensuite référée à la Cour Européenne qui a relevé que ces circonstances sont notamment la complexité de l'affaire, la conduite du procès et des autorités compétentes

En l'espèce, aucune des trois circonstances ne peut justifier un délai de détention provisoire de 4 ans auquel le plaignant soutient qu'il n'est pas raisonnable. La Commission n'est pas de l'avis de l'Etat défendeur qui estime que ce délai est raisonnable dans une procédure où étaient impliqués 21 accusés. En effet, l'implication de 21 accusés ne constitue pas une complexité susceptible de porter une détention préventive à plus de 4 ans. La Commission observe, par ailleurs, que la victime a interjeté appel en 2007 auprès de la Cour Administrative contre le Ministre des Postes et des Télécommunications pour le paiement de ses arriérés de salaire et de dommages-intérêts liés aux poursuites abusives, douleurs et souffrances pour emprisonnement injustifié mais qu'il n'avait pas encore reçu aucune suite en 2013, date de la formulation des observations complémentaires du Plaignant sur le fond. L'Etat défendeur n'en donne pas d'explication bien qu'une opportunité de le faire lui avait été donnée.

Dans l'affaire Odjouoriby Cossi Paul c. / Bénin la Commission a estimé que le fait que le recours devant la Cour d'appel se soit prolongé de façon anormale est contraire à l'esprit et à la lettre de l'article 7(1)(d) susmentionné. Ainsi, la Commission estime que le délai mis par les autorités judiciaires camerounaises pour décider sur la violation des droits de la Victime, sans démontrer les circonstances qui auraient empêché la procédure normale du procès, constitue une violation du droit au procès équitable au sens de l'article 7 (1) (d) de la Charte. Observation de la Commission sur les demandes en réparation.

Le Plaignant allègue qu'il a droit à la réparation par rapport aux violations alléguées. La Commission relève que la Charte africaine ne prévoit pas une disposition spécifique sur la réparation en cas de violation des droits y consacrés. Cependant, conformément à sa jurisprudence, elle note que la violation des droits protégés par la Charte ouvre droit à la réparation. Ainsi par exemple, dans la communication Jean-Marie Atangana Mebara c. République du Cameroun, la Commission a indiqué que la réparation peut prendre des formes variées selon les droits violés et les circonstances de la cause, allant des actions administratives, législatives et judiciaires à la compensation monétaire.

En l'espèce, le plaignant demande une réparation en compensation monétaire d'une valeur globale de 574.680.747 (Cinq Cent Soixante-Quatorze millions Six Cent Quatre-Vingt Mille Sept Cent Quarante Sept FCFA) qu'il répartit en quatre catégories : le salaire de la victime pendant la période d'emprisonnement ; le paiement d'un intérêt de 6% par ans pendant 13 ans ; dommages et intérêts pour poursuites abusives, souffrances et douleurs liées à sa détention injustifiée ; et les frais associés aux différents procédures et refus de payer. La Commission se propose de les analyser une à une. Sur le paiement des arriérés du salaire de la victime pendant la période d'emprisonnement

Le Plaignant demande d'abord le paiement de son salaire correspondant à la période d'Octobre 2000 à décembre 2003 qui équivaut à 13.865.592 FCFA (Treize Millions Huit Cent Soixante Cinq mille cinq cent quatre-vingt-douze FCFA), soit 38 mois x 364.884 FCFA. Ayant constaté des violations de la Charte et surtout, une détention provisoire qui n'a pas respecté les principes établis par la Charte africaine, la Commission relève effectivement que l'Etat responsable de ces violations a l'obligation d'effacer toutes les conséquences de ses actes et ainsi rétablir la victime dans la situation où elle devrait être si ces actes n'avaient pas été commis.

Il en résulte que la Commission consent à une réparation monétaire correspondante aux mois que la victime n'a pas été payée. Il reste cependant à savoir si le montant réel à lui payer équivaut à 13.865.592 FCFA correspondant aux arriérés de 38 mois tel que le réclame le Plaignant, soit 364.884 FCFA par mois. Ceci est important car le principe étant que la réparation doit être juste, adéquate, efficace, suffisante, appropriée, orientée vers la victime et proportionnelle au préjudice subi. La Commission relève que le plaignant ne fournit pas de preuve que les 364.884 FCFA appliquées aux 38 mois étaient réellement le montant de son salaire mensuel au moment de son arrestation. Il aurait, ainsi par exemple, fourni une fiche de paie ou bulletin de son salaire ou encore tout autre document valable pour servir principalement comme justificatif du montant de son salaire mensuel.

En l'absence d'une justification quant au montant du salaire mensuel de la victime, la Commission ne sera pas à mesure de déterminer le montant global des arriérés de salaire que l'Etat défendeur lui doit. En conséquence, tout en consentant au paiement de ces arriérés, la Commission renvoie le Plaignant aux juridictions nationales pour assurer le calcul de ces arriérés de salaire sur base du montant de son salaire mensuel. Sur le paiement d'un intérêt de 6% par an pendant 13 ans

Le Plaignant demande le paiement d'un intérêt de 6% par an pendant 13 ans. Ayant constaté que la détention provisoire n'a pas respecté les normes, un intérêt sur la somme de salaire due à la victime est nécessaire. Cependant, la Commission observe que le Plaignant ne donne pas de base juridique pour les 6% d'intérêt qu'il exige. Là aussi, la Commission renvoie aux juridictions nationales pour assurer le contrôle de ces intérêts conformément au droit national camerounais. Sur le paiement des dommages et intérêts pour poursuites abusives, souffrances et douleurs liés à sa détention injustifiée

Le Plaignant exige également le paiement des dommages et intérêts équivalant à une somme de 500.000.000 FCFA (Cinq Cent Millions de FCFA) pour les poursuites abusives, souffrances et douleurs liées à sa détention injustifiée. La Commission constate que le Plaignant n'a pas établi clairement, avec des pièces justificatives, la valeur des pertes morales et matérielles de la victime. En l'absence de repère mathématique à cette demande pour justifier les 500.000.000 FCFA, la Commission ne peut pas confirmer si cette somme est convenable pour réparer le dommage subi par la victime. Conformément à sa jurisprudence bien établie, la Commission renvoie le plaignant aux juridictions nationales pour l'évaluation de tels dommages et intérêts. Sur la demande des frais associés aux différentes procédures et refus de payer

Le Plaignant demande le paiement d'une somme de 50.000.000 FCFA (Cinquante Millions de FCFA) correspondant aux frais associés aux différentes procédures et refus de payer. La Commission observe qu'ici non plus le Plaignant ne justifie pas ce montant car il ne fournit aucun élément de preuve quant à la valeur réelle des dépenses. Par conséquent, elle renvoie la victime aux juridictions nationales pour assurer ce calcul.
Déclare que : i. Les articles 3 (2) et 5 n'ont pas été violés ii. Les articles 6 et 7 (1) (a) (b) (d) ont été violés

En conséquence, la Commission demande à la République du Cameroun : i. D'accorder à la victime les arriérés de salaires correspondants à sa période de détention. ii. D'accorder à la victime un intérêt sur le montant des arriérés de salaire ; iii. De payer à la victime les dommages et intérêts pour poursuites abusives, souffrances et douleurs liés à sa détention injustifiée ; iv. De rembourser la victime tous les frais associés aux différentes procédures engagées par la victime. Adoptée par la Commission Africaine des Droits de l'Homme et des Peuples lors de sa 72 Session Ordinaire tenue virtuellement du 19 juillet 2022 au 2 Aout 2022

The Secretariat of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Secretariat), received a complaint on 4 October 2013, from Ernest Duga Titanji on behalf of Duga and Co. Law Firm (the Complainant), acting on behalf of Nde Ningo (the Victim).
It is submitted against the Republic of Cameroon (the Respondent State), a State Party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Charter).

The Complainant submits that the Victim is a former civil servant who worked for several years in the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications and held several posts until 24 September 1999. He was never the subject of an investigation or of any reproach with regard to his person.

It is alleged that around 24 September 1999, the Victim was arrested together with Mr Monuchipou Seidou (former Minister of Posts and Telecommunications) and several other persons and was accused and charged with embezzlement of public funds and complicity in the embezzlement of public funds.

The Victim states that he was placed in pre-trial detention for more than 4 years, in very inhuman and degrading conditions, in total violation of his right to the presumption of innocence. At the end of 4 years of detention, the Victim was tried by the Mfoundi High Court and acquitted on 28 November 2003 by decision No. 93/CRIM.
An appeal was lodged against this decision before the Yaoundé Court of Appeal, which upheld the decision of the High Court in a judgment delivered on 27 June 2006.

It is stated that following his acquittal, the Victim sent various letters to the then Minister of Posts and Telecommunications, dated 31 July and 29 January respectively, requesting his reinstatement and the payment of his salary arrears for the 4 years of unlawful and abusive detention.

The Victim submits that the Minister, by letter dated 3 January 2007, refused to pay him his salary arrears and any other sum due, and stated that the Victim was only entitled to a family allowance for the period of his detention.

Subsequently, the Victim, through his lawyer, submitted a request for "Recours Gracieux" (administrative appeal) to the Minister of Posts and Telecommunications, but the latter reiterated his response in the letter of 3 January 2007.

The Complainant alleges that, after exhausting the "Recours gracieux" procedure, the Victim decided to bring the matter before the Administrative Court and paid the various fees set by the court on 14 May 2007 and 4 December 2008, respectively. It was only in 2010 that the Victim's lawyer received written observations from the Ministry concerning the case. Subsequently, correspondence was exchanged with the Ministry, the last dating from 1 July 2010.

The Complainant alleges that to date, there has been no response, despite several reminders sent to the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications. Likewise, he adds, the refusal to reinstate the Victim and to pay him his salary arrears violates a number of rights guaranteed by the Charter.
The Complainant alleges the violation of Articles 3(2) and 5 of the African Charter.

He alleges the violation of Article 6 of the Charter, read together with Article 9 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) and Article 7(1) of the Charter, read together with Articles 14(2) and 3(c) of the ICCPR.
The Complainant further alleges a violation of Article 9(5) of the ICCPR.

The Complainant requests the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Commission) to declare that: i. his rights guaranteed by the African Charter and other international human rights instruments ratified by Cameroon have been violated by the State of Cameroon; ii. the Respondent State must pay him the sum of five hundred and seventy-four million six hundred and eighty thousand seven hundred and forty-seven (574,680,747) CFA francs, which is the total amount of his salary between October 2000 and December 2003, interest of 6% per year for 13 years, damages for abusive prosecution, pain and suffering for abusive detention as well as the costs associated with the various proceedings related to his detention and the refusal to pay.

The Commission seized itself of the Communication during its 54 Ordinary Session held in November 2013. The observations on admissibility were sent to the Complainant on 12 January 2014; they were also duly transmitted to the Respondent State on 20 January 2014.

Not having received the Respondent State's observations on admissibility, the Commission informed both parties, in correspondence dated 26 March 2014, of its intention to proceed to examine the Communication on admissibility on the basis of the information available.

The Communication was declared admissible at the 16 Extraordinary Session held in July 2014. The Respondent State was informed of the decision by Note Verbale dated 4 August 2014. A letter bearing the same date was sent to the Complainant, informing him of the decision and inviting him to submit his arguments on the merits within sixty days from the date of notification.
The Complainant's observations on the merits were transmitted to the Commission by e-mail on 20 October 2014.

In a Note Verbale dated 20 October 2014, the Secretariat transmitted to the Respondent State the observations on the merits received from the Complainant and invited the State to respond within two months.

The Respondent State's observations on the merits being late, the Secretariat informed the State, by Note Verbale dated 18 May 2015, that the Commission would proceed to adopt a decision on the merits if those observations were not received within thirty days following the date of notification.

The Secretariat acknowledged receipt of the Respondent State's observations on the merits by Note Verbale of 3 June 2015. The observations were transmitted to the Complainant by letter bearing the same date.
The Complainant's response to the Respondent State's observations was received by the Commission on 13 July 2015 and transmitted to the Respondent State on 15 July 2015.
The Complainant provides information on the conformity of the Communication with the admissibility requirements set out in Article 56 of the Charter.

Regarding the exhaustion of local remedies, in particular, the Complainant submits that a written complaint was lodged on 7 February 2007 (in accordance with the mandatory administrative procedure under the legislation of the Respondent State) requesting the Minister of Posts and Telecommunications to review his decision to unilaterally suspend the Complainant's salary during the period of his abusive detention. The Complainant also claimed the payment of certain damages for abusive prosecution, pain and suffering for abusive detention. According to the Complainant, all these steps were in vain.

The Complainant states that, in accordance with the procedures in force in Cameroon and since the administrative authority did not respond to his request, on 4 May 2007, the matter was brought before the competent judicial body - the Administrative Chamber of the Supreme Court, which has jurisdiction to deal with administrative matters. The case was registered at the said Court under number 756 of 14 May 2007.

The Complainant further submits that, following the complaint and in acknowledgment of it, the Court set the various fees which were promptly paid each time they were set, on 14 May 2007 and 4 December 2007 respectively. There was no progress until two years later. It was only in 2010 that the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications received the written observations relating to the complaint, after which further correspondence was exchanged, the last dating from 1 July 2010.
The Complainant submits that one could have expected the matter to have been settled, but to date, nothing has been done about it, despite several reminders from the Complainant.
The Complainant finally submits that, even though local remedies exist, they have been unduly prolonged.

The admissibility of Communications submitted to the Commission is governed by the requirements contained in Article 56 of the African Charter. Article 56 sets out seven requirements which must be cumulatively fulfilled for a Communication to be declared admissible.
As indicated above, the Respondent State did not submit its observations on admissibility, despite the opportunity offered to it by Rule 105 of the Commission's Rules of Procedure.

In the present circumstances, and in accordance with the Commission's practice, as set out in the case of Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa v. Republic of Angola, "faced with the State's failure to deal with the complaint filed against it, the African Commission has no choice but to proceed to examine the communication, in accordance with its Rules of Procedure." In the same decision, the Commission reaffirmed its position by holding that: "... it would proceed to examine the Communication on the basis of the observations submitted by the Complainants and the information at its disposal, even if the State has not submitted its observations." Consequently, the Commission must give due consideration to the Complainant's allegations to the extent that they have been sufficiently substantiated.

In the absence of any observations from the Respondent State, the Commission, having carefully examined the information provided by the Complainant, is satisfied that all the requirements set out in Article 56 have been fulfilled.
The identity of the author, Mr Ernest Duga Titanji, has been indicated, in accordance with the provisions of Article 56(1) of the Charter.

Regarding Article 56(2), the Communication is compatible with the provisions of the Charter and of the Constitutive Act of the African Union, as it describes a prima facie case of violation of Articles 3, 5, 6 and 7 of the Charter; it is submitted by the parties entitled to do so, against the Republic of Cameroon, a State Party to the Charter; the violations took place in the territory of the State Party, at a time when the Charter was in force there.
The Communication complies with the requirement of Article 56(3), given that the Commission has not found in it any disparaging or insulting language against the Respondent State or its institutions.

The Commission has found that the Communication is not based exclusively on news disseminated through the mass media, but rather on facts presented by the Complainant, in accordance with Article 56(4) of the Charter.

Regarding Article 56(5) of the Charter, the Commission recalls that this provision of the Charter requires Complainants to exhaust local remedies, if any, unless it is obvious that this procedure is unduly prolonged.

The Complainant has argued in the present case that his attempts to exhaust local remedies were hindered by the procedure which was unduly prolonged in the Respondent State. He submits that he filed a complaint with the Administrative Chamber of the Supreme Court on 14 May 2007 and paid the required court fees, but the case had not been heard at the time of the events.

It should be recalled that what constitutes a "procedure that is unduly prolonged" under Article 56(5) has not been defined by the African Commission. There is therefore no rule applied by the Commission to determine whether a procedure has been unduly prolonged. The Commission deals with each case on its merits, taking into account factors such as the very nature of the complaint, the political situation of the country, its judicial history, among others.

In Zimbabwe Lawyers for Human Rights v. Zimbabwe, the Commission held that "the exception provided for in Article 56(5) requires that the procedure must not only be prolonged, but also "unduly" so. For the Commission, the expression Unduly means "excessively" in an unjustifiable manner". Thus, if there is a justifiable reason for prolonging a case, it cannot be described as "undue", for example where the country finds itself in a war or civil conflict, or if the delay is partly caused by the victim, his family or his representatives".

In the present communication, the Commission notes that the case was pending before the domestic courts for a period of seven (7) years, before the Complainant approached the Commission. The Commission also notes that no reason has been given for this excessive delay. The Complainant explained that he had followed up the case with the Court on several occasions but received no response. It therefore appears to the Commission that the delay in dealing with the Complainant's case by the domestic courts has not been justified.

It was also explained that the suspension of the Complainant's salary during the period of his trial and the refusal to restore his rights after his acquittal plunged the Complainant and his family into destitution, forcing them to beg for food from their Christian community. One could have expected the matter to be dealt with promptly, given that the Complainant's case concerns his very survival and that of his family. The fact that there has been no hearing of the case, after seven years, manifestly constitutes a procedure that is unduly prolonged, in the circumstances.
For this reason, the Commission considers that the local remedies procedure has been unduly prolonged, and that there was no obligation on the part of the Complainant to exhaust them.

Regarding Article 56(6) of the Charter, the Commission considers that the Communication was submitted within a reasonable time, after the complainant realised that the procedure was being unduly prolonged at the domestic level.

The Commission has no information to the effect that the subject matter of the Communication had been settled through other international dispute settlement procedures, in accordance with Article 56(7) of the Charter. This requirement is therefore met.
In view of the foregoing, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights declares the Communication admissible.

The complainant alleges that the State of Cameroon violated Article 3(2) of the Charter, which protects the right to equal protection of the law. In support of his allegation, he points out that the Mfoundi High Court and the Yaoundé Court of Appeal are clear actors in this violation by virtue of their decisions, which state that the charges against the Complainant were unfounded. He reiterates that if the victim had benefited from the presumption of innocence and, consequently, obtained provisional release, he would not have spent 4 years in detention without any justification.

Referring to Article 2 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), the complainant indicates that any person who has been deprived of liberty must be entitled to an effective remedy and that his rights must be determined by a competent judicial, administrative or legislative authority or any administrative authority. The Complainant submits that although the Respondent State incorporated Article 2 of the ICCPR into the Cameroonian Code of Criminal Procedure of 2005 in its sections 236 and 237 on compensation for unlawful detention, the remedies in this case remain ineffective.
The Complainant reiterates that Article 3(2) of the Charter is non-derogable and must be respected in all circumstances to enable every person to enjoy the other rights prescribed in the Charter.

He indicates that the victim used all administrative and judicial remedies since 2007 for the restoration of his rights which were suspended by unjustified acts of the State on the one hand, and for the prejudice suffered as a result of unjustified detention on the other. He reiterates that his claims have not been redressed after 7 years of seeking justice. He argues that where the available remedies are unduly prolonged, they must be interpreted as non-existent. Consequently, he urges the Commission to adopt the reasoning it developed in the case of Bissangou v. Republic of Congo to find a violation of Article 3 of the Charter.

The complainant alleges that the treatment to which the victim was subjected by way of detention for more than 4 years is sufficient to be considered degrading. He also adds that the suspension of his salary throughout the period of the trial, leaving him no means of subsistence, is cruel, inhuman and degrading. Worse still, he points out, even after having been tried, discharged and acquitted, the mere fact of refusing to reinstate him in his position is a clear sign of humiliation in the eyes of society. His honour and that of his family were degraded, given that they were forced to live like beggars at the mercy of the goodwill of people of good faith.

The complainant insists, stating that the victim had never in his life been reduced to the position where he was obliged to beg for food from the Church. According to him, had he been reinstated in his original position, he could have gained a certain level of credibility in society. He finally concludes that this conduct is in contradiction with the minimum standards described in the United Nations principles for the protection of all persons under any form of detention or imprisonment, in particular Principles 1 and 6, as well as the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights in its Article 7.

On the basis of all these elements, he implores the Commission to follow its reasoning in Communications 97/93 John K Modise v. Botswana; John D. Ouko v. Kenya (2000); International Pen and Others (on behalf of Saro Wiwa) v. Nigeria to find a violation of Article 5 of the Charter by the Republic of Cameroon.

The complainant alleges that the proceedings brought against him, which materialised in his detention and imprisonment for 4 years, are a violation of Article 6 of the Charter and Article 9 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and, consequently, violate the right to liberty. According to him, every person is presumed innocent until declared guilty by a competent Court or Tribunal. He reiterates that he could have benefited from release on bail. The latter, he insists, makes it possible to prevent the State from being responsible for the violation of the right to liberty each time the accused is found not guilty of the charges brought against him.

The complainant indicates that, moreover, the Cameroonian Code of Criminal Procedure of 2005 specifies in its Article 221 that the period of pre-trial detention must be fixed by the investigating judge in the warrant and that it may not exceed six (6) months. This period may be extended by a reasoned order for twelve (12) months at most in the case of a felony and six (6) months in the case of a misdemeanour.

The complainant concludes that in light of all the foregoing, the Respondent State has not only violated the provisions of national law, but also those of the African Charter and those of international human rights law.

Referring to Article 9, paragraph 5 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which stipulates that any individual who has been the victim of unlawful arrest or detention has the right to reparation, the complainant points out that the State of Cameroon violated his right to compensation. He alleges that he has repeatedly tried to seek compensation but in vain. He asks the Commission to refer to its jurisprudence in Communications 64/92, 68/92, and 78/92 Achuthan and Others and in Communication 292/2004 Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa v. Republic of Angola to finally find a violation of the right to compensation by the Cameroonian State.

The complainant alleges that the Respondent State violated the right to respect for human dignity as described in Article 5 of the Charter and Article 10, paragraphs 1 and 2(a) of the ICCPR. He points out that Kondengui prison is internationally recognised as overcrowded and that it does not separate convicted from unconvicted prisoners. According to the Complainant, the detainees are mixed together and the only form of distinction that exists is the separation between male and female detainees, and to a lesser extent, minors and adults.

The complainant alleges the violation of the right to a fair trial. In support of his allegation, he points out that the victim was denied the right to appeal because the remedy he sought was unduly prolonged. He insists in particular that the appeal of 14 May 2007 was lodged before the administrative branch of the Supreme Court.

He submits that he received the written observations of the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications in 2010 with the last exchange on 1 July 2010. He reiterates that since that day, nothing has been done to move the case forward despite many reminders. He implores the Commission to follow its reasoning in Communication 59/91 to find that the appeal was unduly prolonged.

He also alleges that the victim's right to the presumption of innocence was violated. In support of his allegation, he points out above all that the victim's pre-trial detention for a period of more than four years, during which he was held in very inhuman and degrading conditions without regard to his status, and above all in the same cells as convicted persons, is a violation of his right to the presumption of innocence.

The complainant also submits that the victim's right to be tried within a reasonable time by an independent Tribunal was violated. He indicates that the essence of this right is to prevent the victim from undergoing prolonged detention so as not to exacerbate his suffering and the loss of his liberty when he is finally found not guilty of the offence. He concludes that no one could claim that four years is not an excessive period. In support of his allegation, he refers to Communication No. 708/1996 of Lewis v. Jamaica before the United Nations Human Rights Committee, where 3 years were found excessive, and to the Communication Pegnoulle (on behalf of Mazou) v. Cameroon before the Commission, which deals with Article 7(1)(d) of the Charter protecting the right to be tried within a reasonable time.

He concludes that from the foregoing, Articles 7(1) of the Charter and 14, paragraphs 2 and 3(c) of the ICCPR have been violated by the State of Cameroon. He therefore requests compensation of 574,680,747 (Five Hundred and Seventy-Four million Six Hundred and Eighty thousand Seven Hundred and Forty Seven) CFA francs. On the alleged violation of Article 3(2) of the Charter and Article 2(3) of the ICCPR (Right to equality before the law and to equal protection of the law and the right to an effective remedy)

The Respondent State submits that the right to equality and non-discrimination implies that identical treatment be accorded to persons in similar situations. According to the Respondent State, the Complainant has not provided evidence of different treatment compared to other persons in the same situation.

The Respondent State thus insists that the Complainant cannot invoke the application of the Bissangou v. Congo case where the Commission held that the non-execution of a judgment by the Minister of Finance constituted a violation of the principle of equality before the law. According to the Respondent State, the Complainant has not provided evidence of differentiated treatment of the victim compared to other persons in a situation identical to his.

The Respondent State points out that in invoking the violation of the right to an effective remedy, the Complainant refers in particular to Articles 236 and 237 of the CPP without indicating the steps he has taken to seize the Commission established for that purpose. It indicates that, moreover, this procedure is applicable to cases of abusive detention and that this is not the case here. On the violation of Article 5 of the Charter and Articles 7 and 10 of the ICCPR (Right not to be subjected to torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment)

The Respondent State submits that pre-trial detention is not prohibited by the Charter, provided that it is carried out under specific conditions and considers that these conditions were respected in this case. In support of its position, it points out that for treatment to be considered "degrading", it must be motivated by the desire to humiliate. However, according to the Respondent State, the decision to suspend the victim's salary was taken in the context of the judicial proceedings brought against the victim for embezzlement of public funds and there was no intention to humiliate him. It adds, moreover, that the care of detained persons is the responsibility of the State and that the Victim benefited from it during his detention. It also says that the victim receives a pension from the State.

As for the allegations about the conditions of detention in Kondengui prison, the Respondent State considers that the Complainant limits himself to providing general information without substantiating his claims and demonstrating the shortcomings in the treatment accorded to him. It points to the example of a communication Bailey v. Jamaica submitted to the Human Rights Committee where the author had relied on the report of a non-governmental organisation denouncing the conditions of detention in a penitentiary; the Committee considered that such a document could not on its own support the allegations of violation of Article 10.1 of the ICCPR.

The Respondent State submits that the arbitrariness invoked by the Complainant in relation to the victim's arrest or pre-trial detention cannot be applicable to the present case. According to it, the limitation of the duration of pre-trial detention provided for by Article 221 of the CPP to which the Complainant refers cannot be applicable in the present case because the Code of Criminal Procedure came into force on 1 January 2007, that is, 3 years after the acquittal of the author of the Communication.

With regard to the allegation that the right to the presumption of innocence was violated, the Respondent State indicates that pre-trial detention is not necessarily contradictory to the presumption of innocence, the measure having to be based on grounds and to follow a procedure previously determined by law. It concludes, consequently, that the victim's detention cannot be characterised as arbitrary.

On the allegation that the victim would be entitled to reparation in accordance with Article 9(5); the Respondent State submits that his detention is lawful and cannot be the subject of an action for reparation on the basis of this provision

The Respondent State alleges that the right to the presumption of innocence on which the complainant relies to allege the violation of the right to a fair trial was not violated. In support of its position, it indicates that despite his detention, the courts fairly examined his case and ultimately acquitted him.
The Respondent State also considers that 4 years of proceedings, from the investigation to the judicial phase, cannot objectively be considered unreasonable.

In his reply to the Respondent State's observations, the Complainant gives a brief description of the facts and of the proceedings already undertaken to date before responding to the State's conclusions. The Complainant's additional arguments can be summarised as follows:

The Complainant alleges that the Respondent State deliberately refused to respond to the facts he raised by simply arguing that he (the Complainant) has not proved how his case is different from that of others. He reiterates instead that if the State has violated the rights of some of its citizens or if the violated rights concern several persons who have not filed a complaint, he would still be entitled to file a complaint for his case. He supports his view by indicating that it is not his role to ask others whether they are interested in filing a complaint to seek reparation for violated rights.

On the second argument whereby the State alleges that the Complainant has not shown the steps the victim has taken to seek reparation, the Complainant refers the Respondent State to the reading of the Commission's decision on admissibility to see whether it invented the facts and the steps taken by the victim to exhaust local remedies. He submits that this argument is raised belatedly and attempts to introduce the exception or defence of non-exhaustion of local remedies. He considers that this point was analysed exhaustively by the Commission in its decision on admissibility.

The complainant reiterates that if the victim had benefited from the presumption of innocence and, consequently, release on bail, he would not have spent four unjustified years in detention. He asks the Commission to follow its own reasoning from the case of Bissangou v. Republic of Congo (2006)

The Complainant reaffirms his argument that, in the case of pre-trial detention, when it is found that there has been an error and the person is not found guilty, he is entitled to reparation and, where his salary has been suspended, it will be reinstated retroactively.

The complainant rejects the argument by which the Respondent State alleges that the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure of Cameroon invoked to support his argument are not applicable to the present case because this Code came into force on 1 January 2007 whereas the complainant was acquitted in 2004. According to him, the appeal decision came after the promulgation of the Cameroonian Code of Criminal Procedure and the problem remains unresolved by the Cameroonian State, 10 years after the promulgation of the law which is supposed to punish arbitrary and abusive arrests. According to him, this would mean that the Respondent State has put in place a for to deceive the vigilance of the international Community.

He reiterates that at the very least the State should respect the international instruments it has duly ratified and to which the complainant refers, in particular Article 6 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights

On the Respondent State's response that this right to compensation applies to cases of unlawful detention and that the victim cannot benefit from this compensation because his detention was not unlawful, the complainant reiterates that he has sufficiently elaborated his arguments and that he still considers that he is entitled to compensation. He finally returns to his earlier observations.

The complainant is surprised by the State's response which seems to conclude that the 4-year duration of the proceedings brought against the victim before the Mfoundi Court is reasonable because the case involved 21 other persons. In this regard, the complainant alleges that the Respondent State forgets that it appealed an acquittal decision that had been taken by its own courts, which prolonged the proceedings unnecessarily. He also recalls that the case is still pending 12 years later. While returning to his earlier observations on the merits, the Complainant indicates that his arguments are based on Articles 7(1) of the Charter and 14(3) and (4) of the ICCPR combined.

The complainant recalls that he claims payment of his salary arrears from October 2000 to December 2003 equivalent to 36 months x 364,884 CFA francs = 10,815,155 CFA francs, as well as payment of interest of 6% per year for 13 years (13,865,592 x 6% x 13) = 10,815,155 CFA francs. He submits that this claim is clearly provided for by the laws of the Republic of Cameroon and that if the case pending against Cameroon had been heard (he insists that the case has not yet been heard), this sum of money would have been awarded to the victim.

The complainant relies above all on the provisions of Decree No. 94/199 establishing the Code of the Public Service of Cameroon of 7 October 1994 to explain that after his acquittal, the victim was entitled to have his rights restored retroactively.

Before any analysis of the complainant's allegations, the Commission finds it important to recall the scope of its competence under the Charter. Indeed, in the present Communication, the Complainant requests the Commission to find a violation of the provisions of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights in parallel with the provisions of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR). He also requests the Commission to find a violation of Article 9(5) of the ICCPR as an autonomous violation.

Unlike the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights, which is vested with the competence to interpret and apply the Charter, the Protocol establishing it and any other relevant human rights instrument ratified by the States concerned under Article 3(1) of the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights on the Establishment of an African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights, this is not the case for the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights. Indeed, Article 45 of the African Charter empowers the Commission to ensure the protection of human and peoples' rights under conditions laid down by the Charter and limits its interpretation to the provisions of the Charter.

It follows that the Commission is not competent to interpret the provisions of any other instrument including the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, the violation of which the complainant invokes.

However, in order to fulfil its mission of interpreting the Charter, the Commission is empowered to draw inspiration from international law on human and peoples' rights under Article 60 of the Charter. It may in particular draw inspiration from the provisions of the various African instruments on human and peoples' rights, the provisions of the Charter of the United Nations, the Charter of the Organization of African Unity, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the provisions of other instruments adopted by the United Nations and by African countries in the field of human and peoples' rights, as well as the provisions of various instruments adopted within the specialised institutions of the United Nations of which the parties to the present Charter are members.

Thus, in application of this principle clearly established by the Charter, the Commission cannot provide an interpretation of, or find a violation of, the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights but may, rather, draw inspiration from it. In this perspective and in this case, the Commission will analyse the alleged violations of the provisions of the Charter drawing inspiration, where necessary, from the provisions of this ICCPR and of other human rights protection instruments but will not be able to rule on the violation of provisions of the latter, regardless of whether the Complainant has invoked the autonomous or joint violation of this Convention.

Article 3(2) provides that "Every individual shall be entitled to equal protection of the law". In view of the Complainant's allegations, it is important for the Commission to determine the meaning of this right provided for in Article 3(2) of the Charter.

In the Communication Spilg and Mack & DITSHWANELO (on behalf of Lehlohonolo Bernard Kobedi) v. Botswana, the Commission indicated that the right to equal protection of the law envisaged by Article 3 of the African Charter consists of the right of all persons to have the same access to the law and the courts, and to be treated in the same way by the law and the courts both at the level of procedures and of the very substance of the law. So described, this right is a guarantee that no person or class of persons may be denied the same protection of the laws enjoyed by other persons or other classes in like circumstances in their life, liberty and property.

The African Commission therefore considers that, for there to be a violation of Article 3 of the African Charter, it must be shown that the victim of the alleged violation did not benefit from the same protection or the same treatment as that normally accorded to other persons in similar circumstances. In the case of Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa v. Angola, the Commission emphasised this aspect by indicating that for a Complainant to successfully bring a complaint under Article 3 of the Charter, he must prove that the Respondent State had not accorded the victims the same treatment accorded to others, or that it had accorded favourable treatment to others in the same situation as the victims.

In this case, and in view of the previous considerations, the Commission is called upon to analyse whether the victim faced such a difference in treatment. After analysis of the arguments and elements submitted by the Complainant, the Commission is of the view, as is the Respondent State, that the Complainant has not proved to what extent the victim of the present Communication was treated differently from other persons in the same situation as him. In particular, to justify that there was a violation of the right to equal protection before the law, the Complainant invokes the absence or lack of will of the State of Cameroon to redress the misery and suffering of NDE NINGO after his trial and acquittal on spurious charges that had been brought against him.

Without wishing to deny the right of every person to be compensated recognised for every victim of a human rights violation, the Commission notes that this argument is not relevant to justify the violation of the right to equal protection before the law as intended by the spirit of the Charter in its Article 3(2). The Complainant would have shown that this absence or lack of will on the part of the State of Cameroon to compensate the victim was selective with regard to him and that, above all, other victims in the same conditions as him benefited from this compensation.

The complainant rejects the Respondent State's argument that he (the Complainant) has not proved how his case is different from that of others and considers this argument to be irrelevant. He insists that, if other persons concerned by the violated rights did not wish to file a complaint, he would still be justified in filing a complaint for what concerns him. The Commission considers that this reasoning is also not valid to find that there was a violation of Article 3(2). Indeed, every person is obviously entitled and justified to file a complaint whenever he considers that his rights are violated even if these violations concern other persons, regardless of whether the latter express their wish to seize the competent judicial authorities or not.

In this case, what would have been of interest to the Commission would simply be proof of a difference in treatment of which the Complainant was a victim. The Commission considers that, even in the absence of other complaints on similar situations, the Complainant can still prove that a law was applied differently and to his detriment compared to others. Indeed, as the Commission has already explained in the case of Bissangou v. Republic of Congo, equal protection of the law, guaranteed in paragraph 2 of Article 3, is concerned with the implementation of the law and applies when the Complainant's rights are implemented unequally.

Thus, the Complainant would, for example, have proved that other persons in the same situation as the victim benefited from their compensation or simply that the Respondent State showed its willingness to restore them to their rights. In the absence of such proof, it considers that Article 3(2) has not been violated in this respect.

On the Complainant's request to the Commission to apply the reasoning of Communication Bissango v. Democratic Republic of Congo to the present case to find a violation of Article 3 of the Charter, the Commission notes that the facts in the two cases are different. Indeed, in the Bissango case, the Minister of Economy, Finance and Budget refused to execute a judicial decision which ordered the Republic of Congo and the Brazzaville city hall jointly to pay the Complainant a sum of money as damages. The Commission considered that it was incumbent on the aforementioned Minister to honour the judgment by virtue of the principles of the separation of powers and the principle of res judicata. It also found that there were victims who had been compensated and concluded that there was a violation of Article 3 of the Charter.
In this case, it has not been demonstrated that certain victims were compensated. Hence the Commission concludes that Article 3(2) has not been violated.

Article 5 of the Charter provides: "Every individual shall have the right to the respect of the dignity inherent in a human being and to the recognition of his legal status. All forms of exploitation and degradation of man particularly slavery, slave trade, torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment and treatment shall be prohibited". The Complainant's allegations as to the violation of this article concern two main violations: the violation of the right to dignity inherent in the human person and the violation of the right against torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment.

The Commission considers that the two rights are intimately linked. Indeed, dignity is a concept around which the prohibition of torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment is founded. The Commission is thus of the view that cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment necessarily violates human dignity. In view of the complainant's allegations, the Commission proposes to analyse the two rights one by one in relation to the facts described in the present Communication. On the alleged violation of the right to respect for the dignity inherent in the human person

In the case of Purohit and Moore v. Gambia (The), the Commission noted that human dignity is a fundamental right to which all human beings must be entitled without any discrimination whatsoever, regardless of their mental capacities or incapacities, as the case may be. Consequently, it considered it a natural right that every human being is obliged to respect, by all means, and which also confers on every human being the duty to respect it.

Finally, in the case of Open Society Justice Initiative v. Côte d'Ivoire the Commission summarised the scope of the concept of dignity in the following terms: "Dignity is therefore the soul of the African human rights system and it shares it with all other systems but also with all civilised human societies. Dignity is consubstantial, intrinsic and inherent to the human person. In other words, when the individual has lost his dignity, it is his human nature itself that is called into question to the point where he is liable to question the merit of continuing to belong to human society"

So described, it is understandable that human dignity is the very centre of what makes up the human personality. Thus, for example, in the case of John K Modise v. Botswana, the Commission observed that the victim "was forced to live for eight years in the "homeland" of Bophuthatswana, and for a further seven years in the "No-Man's Land", a border zone between the former South African homeland of Bophuthatswana and Botswana. These acts exposed him to suffering in his person and deprived him of his dignity, in violation of the right to protection against cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment set out in Article 5 of the Charter."

In the Communication Purohit and Moore v. Gambia also, the Commission found that by labelling persons suffering from mental illness as "lunatics" and "idiots", the Lunatics Detention Act (LDA) dehumanises them and denies them all forms of dignity, in violation of Article 5 of the African Charter.

In this case, the Complainant alleges that the poor conditions of detention in which the victim found himself in Kondengui prison constitute a violation of the dignity inherent in his person. On this allegation, the Commission is of the view, as is the Respondent State, that the Complainant limits himself to providing general information without substantiating his claims and demonstrating the shortcomings in the treatment accorded to the victim. Thus, for example, in his reasoning, the complainant indicates that "it is indisputable that the facilities of Kondengui prison [...] do not distinguish between convicted and unconvicted persons because it [Kondengui prison] is well known throughout the world as being overcrowded".

The Commission considers this assertion to be a gratuitous statement based on the mass media and unsupported by evidence and considers that it cannot constitute a legal argument. Thus, in the absence of tangible evidence of the facts described, the Commission concludes that Article 5 has not been violated in this respect. On the alleged violation of the prohibition of torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment.

The Complainant considers that the treatment to which he was subjected by way of detention for more than 5 years and the suspension of his salary throughout the period of detention without leaving him any means of subsistence is cruel, inhuman and degrading.

The Charter does not define the notion of torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment. In the absence of a definition in the Charter, the Commission can only draw inspiration from other international human rights instruments to understand its scope. This is the case, for example, of General Comment No. 20 of the United Nations Human Rights Committee. In interpreting Article 7 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which prohibits torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment, the Committee indicated that this article "relates not only to acts that cause physical pain but also to acts that cause mental suffering".

The Commission also considers that the acts covered by Article 5 of the Charter do not concern only acts causing serious physical or psychological suffering but also acts which humiliate the person or force him against his will or conscience. This is also the view of the United Nations Human Rights Committee, which considers that "the prohibition must extend to corporal punishment, including excessive chastisement ordered as a punishment for a crime or as an educative or disciplinary measure".

It remains, however, to be seen what the criteria are for identifying punishment or treatment that may be characterised as torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment. In the case of Ireland v. United Kingdom, the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) considered that "to fall within the scope of Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment, ill-treatment must attain a minimum level of severity.

According to this Court, the assessment of this minimum is relative by its very nature; "it depends on all the circumstances of the case, such as the duration of the treatment, its physical or mental effects and, in some cases, the sex, age and state of health of the victim, etc.".

Along the same lines, the United Nations Human Rights Committee has not considered it necessary to draw up a list of prohibited acts or to establish sharp distinctions between the different kinds of prohibited punishment or treatment but has rather indicated that these distinctions depend on the nature, purpose and severity of the treatment applied.

In the absence of these criteria of identification, the treatments already considered by the Commission as constituting torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment may serve as an example for the understanding of what may be classified in this category in the case of detention. Thus, for example, in a series of communications against Mauritania, the Commission had to consider allegations of ill-treatment or abuse against prisoners including beatings, burns, electric shocks, burial alive in sand until death and the rape of women. It considered that these treatments taken together or in isolation constitute proof of a widespread use of torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment.

In this case, the Commission is called upon to analyse whether the facts alleged by the Complainant are such as to be considered cruel, inhuman or degrading. In particular, the Complainant submits that the detention for 4 years and the suspension of his salary during the period of the trial without leaving him any means of subsistence is cruel, inhuman and degrading. After analysis of the parties' arguments, the Commission is of the view that the facts as presented by the Complainant cannot be analysed as either torture or cruel or inhuman treatment within the meaning of Article 5 of the Charter. Indeed, the Commission finds nothing in the arguments or elements presented by the Complainant that can show that the victim experienced suffering of the degree inherent in these notions as the Commission has described them above.

As already explained above, the nature, purpose and severity of the treatment are key elements in determining the forms of prohibited punishment or treatment. Thus, for example, the Commission notes that although reprehensible in the eyes of the law and of the fundamental principles of human rights protection, the long pre-trial detention of 4 years to which the victim was subjected does not have the severity of inhuman or degrading treatment, still less of torture within the meaning of Article 5. In this case, it has not been proved that the purpose pursued by the Respondent State in keeping the victim in detention for 4 years was to humiliate him. What is more, the Commission observes that the degree of severity of this treatment with regard to the victim is not such as to provoke a feeling of fear, anguish and inferiority capable of humiliating the victim, of debasing him or of breaking his physical or moral resistance as described by the European Court of Human Rights. The Commission is of the view that during his detention, although relatively long, the victim did not undergo acts of treatment such as to cause physical and/or mental pain of a certain severity.

As another ground, the Complainant alleges that the suspension of the victim's salary throughout the period of the trial and the refusal to pay him retroactively after his acquittal constitutes a cruel, inhuman and degrading act given that he was reduced to begging and concludes that the act is degrading for a person of his stature. As already indicated previously, the degree of severity of the treatment inflicted is an important criterion in order to assess its degrading nature.

In this case, the Complainant seems to rely on the stature of the victim to show the severity of the treatment suffered by the victim. The European Commission of Human Rights had to consider the question of the rank of the victim in relation to the definition of the term "degrading treatment" in Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights. In the case of East African Asians v. United Kingdom, it first returned to the overall philosophy surrounding the prohibition of degrading treatment, namely the degree of severity of the treatment. In particular, it noted that the term "degrading treatment" [...] indicates that the general object of the provision is to prevent interferences with human dignity of a particularly serious nature. It thus concluded that an action which lowers a person in rank, position or reputation cannot be regarded as degrading treatment within the meaning of Article 3 unless it reaches a certain level of severity.

In view of these observations, the Commission does not find this ground convincing either for three main reasons. First, the Complainant does not provide sufficient elements to prove that the victim had a particular stature in his society. Indeed, the Commission does not see how being an employee of the Ministry confers a particular stature. Second, the victim's salary was suspended during the period of his pre-trial detention and his release coincided with his retirement age. It is observed, indeed, that after his acquittal followed by his release on 28 November 2003, a pension was paid to him on 11 December 2003, that is, 2 weeks after his release, as appears from Order No. 005923/MFPRA/DGC/SDLD/SAPF/BPAF which admitted Mr Nde Ningo to retirement.

Finally, the Commission also notes that during his period of detention, the victim was entitled to the family pension. This appears from the Complainant's brief which indicates that when the victim sent a second letter to the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications to request payment of the salary arrears corresponding to his period of detention after the decision of the Court of Appeal which confirmed his acquittal, the Minister categorically refused to pay his arrears, arguing that the victim was entitled to a family allowance during his period of detention.

All these observations suggest that the treatment resulting from the non-payment of arrears to the victim is not of a pronounced severity such as to constitute a degrading act as defined by the Commission in the preceding paragraphs because the victim benefited from or was entitled to certain allowances.
It follows that Article 5 has not been violated

The Complainant alleges the violation of Article 6 of the Charter which provides that: "Every individual shall have the right to liberty and to the security of his person. No one may be deprived of his freedom except for reasons and conditions previously laid down by law. In particular, no one may be arbitrarily arrested or detained". This article recognises and protects both the right to liberty of the person and the right to security of the person. Both rights are fundamental because they influence the enjoyment of other rights. Indeed, as the United Nations Human Rights Committee indicated in its general comment No. 35; the liberty and security of a person are valuable in themselves and also because the deprivation of liberty and the denial of the right to security of the person have historically been means of impeding the enjoyment of other rights.

In the view of the Commission, the provisions of this article can be summarised in a single sentence: arrests and detentions must be carried out in accordance with the law. In the case of Amnesty International and Others v. Sudan, the Commission indicated that Article 6 must be interpreted so as to permit arrests only in the exercise of the powers normally vested in law enforcement authorities in a democratic society. However, compliance with the law during the arrest process and during the period of detention is not in itself sufficient to satisfy the requirements of Article 6; it is also necessary that these laws be acceptable in a democratic society.

Thus, for example, in the above-mentioned case against Sudan, the Commission found that the wording of the decree which allowed arrests for vague reasons and on suspicion, and not proven acts, was not in conformity with the spirit of the African Charter. Finally, the prohibition of arbitrariness also requires that the limitation of liberty in the context of arrests or detentions be carried out under the authority and supervision of persons who, from a procedural point of view, are competent to certify it with full independence.

In this case, the question is whether the victim's detention was carried out in accordance with the law and the principles established by the Charter in its Article 5. Indeed, the Complainant alleges that the proceedings brought against him, which materialised in his detention and imprisonment for 4 years, are a violation of his right to liberty. He considers that he could have benefited from release on bail and that in the absence of such release, his right to the presumption of innocence was violated.

The Commission observes that the Victim was arrested on 24 September 1999 and remained in prison until his acquittal by the Court on 28 November 2003, that is, more than four years of pre-trial detention. The Commission recalls that liberty is the principle and detention the exception. Detention is justified only in specific situations where the public interest outweighs the right to liberty of the person guaranteed by Article 6.

This was particularly emphasised by the Commission in the Principles and Guidelines on the Right to a Fair Trial and Legal Assistance in Africa, which indicated that "unless there is sufficient evidence making it necessary to take measures to prevent a person arrested and charged with a criminal offence from absconding, influencing witnesses or posing a clear and serious risk to others, States shall ensure that the said person is not placed in pre-trial detention. In the case under analysis, the Respondent State does not show how the release of the victim would have been a clear and serious threat to society or the possibility of the victim absconding.

On the complainant's argument that the Cameroonian civil code sets in its Article 221 the period of pre-trial detention at 6 months extendable by 12 months, the Commission is of the view, as is the Respondent State, that the Civil Code to which the complainant refers was adopted after the victim's release, on 27 July 2005, that is, 1 year and 8 months after his release. Consequently, this Code cannot serve as a basis to prove that the pre-trial detention exceeded the legal time limits.

However, the Respondent State produces no argument to contradict the allegation that the pre-trial detention lasted more than 4 years nor any reasons that would justify detention of such duration although the opportunity had been given to it. The Commission is of the view that a detention of more than 4 years, as is the case in the situation under analysis, cannot be considered pre-trial and that, consequently, it is an abusive pre-trial detention.
It follows that Article 6 of the Charter has been violated.

The complainant alleges the violation of Article 7(1) of the Charter and Article 14(2) and (3) of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. Both provisions protect the right to a fair trial. For reasons already indicated, the Commission's analysis as to the violation of this right will be limited to the violation of Article 7(1) of the Charter.

Article 7(1) provides: "1. Every individual shall have the right to have his cause heard. This comprises: (a) the right to an appeal to competent national organs against acts of violating his fundamental rights as recognized and guaranteed by conventions, laws, regulations and customs in force; (b) the right to be presumed innocent until proved guilty by a competent court or tribunal; (c) the right to defence, including the right to be defended by counsel of his choice; (d) the right to be tried within a reasonable time by an impartial court or tribunal."

In this case, the complainant alleges the violation of the right to appeal to competent national organs, of the right to be presumed innocent and of the right to be tried within a reasonable time by an impartial court or tribunal. The Commission proposes to analyse them one by one according to the circumstances of the case.

In this sense, the right to have one's cause heard includes the right to bring a case before a court as well as the right to appeal a decision of first instance before higher courts. Thus, for example, in the case of Purohit and Moore v. Gambia, the Commission concluded that the fact that the Lunatics Detention Act (LDA) contained no provision on review or appeal against a judicial order of committal or any remedy against a committal decided on the basis of an erroneous diagnosis or treatment, or the failure of Gambian law to allow the mentally ill to challenge their detention, is a violation of Article 7(1)(a) and (c). This suggests that the guarantees of Article 7(1)(a) go beyond hearing in a normal context of judicial proceedings or decisions to include the content of the laws guaranteeing the right of appeal.

The qualifier "competent" in the provisions of Article 7(1)(a) is particularly sensitive because it includes elements such as the expertise of the judges and the justice inherent in the laws which govern them. In other words, the availability of remedies is not sufficient in itself; it is also necessary that these remedies be effective and capable of delivering a judgment within the required or reasonable time, as the case may be. In the Norbert Zongo case, the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights indicated that the right to have one's cause heard by the competent national courts implies, among other things, that the available judicial remedies be both effective and capable of settling disputes within a reasonable time.

In this case, the issue is whether the appeal lodged by the victim before the Administrative Court was effective and conclusive within a reasonable time. The Commission observes that the victim lodged an appeal on 14 May 2007 before the Administrative Court for payment of his salary arrears and damages linked to abusive prosecution, pain and suffering for unjustified imprisonment. The exchange of observations between the parties ended on 1 July 2010 and at the time of receipt of the communication in 2013, there had been no new development. Even at the time of formulation of the Complainant's observations on the Respondent State's conclusions on 10 July 2015, that is, 12 years later, the case was still pending.

The Respondent State gives no reason that would justify this manifest delay by the Administrative Court in settling the dispute. Yet, as the Commission held in the Principles and Guidelines on the Right to a Fair Trial and Legal Assistance in Africa, "the right of appeal must give rise to an effective and timely review of the case". In the absence of an effective remedy, the Commission concludes that the right to appeal to competent courts as defined in Article 7(1)(a) has been violated.

The complainant also alleges the violation of the right to the presumption of innocence. This right specifically implies that a person accused of a crime must be considered innocent until his guilt is established. Consequently, he must be treated as innocent in all situations, whether within or outside judicial proceedings. Thus, for example, in the case of Civil Liberties Organisation, Legal Defence Centre, Legal Defence and Assistance Project v. Nigeria, the Commission indicated that the presumption of innocence was a "fundamental principle preventing the accused from being treated by the public authorities as if they were already guilty of an offence before their guilt is established by a competent court". It is therefore the responsibility of all public authorities to refrain from prejudging an accused before the outcome of a trial.

So understood, the presumption of innocence implies a need to determine whether an accused person is innocent or guilty as quickly as possible. Thus, for example, in the case of Haregewoin Gabre-Selassie and IHRDA v. Ethiopia, the Commission found that the prolonged imprisonment without conviction of the victims for a period of approximately 16 years clearly violates their right to the presumption of innocence in that it has become like a punishment before the pronouncement of judgment. It follows that judicial proceedings must be as rapid as possible, in particular where the accused is in prison, to prevent detention from becoming a punishment before judgment.

In this case, the victim's pre-trial detention lasted four years and his release took place after his acquittal by the Court. Considering the length of this detention before judgment, the Commission considers that it was based on a presumption of guilt on the part of the authorities of the Respondent State and, consequently, contrary to the principle of the presumption of innocence.

The Commission does not share the view of the Respondent State, which considers that the victim's right to the presumption of innocence was not violated because despite his detention, the courts fairly examined his case and ultimately acquitted him. Indeed, in this sense, respect for the presumption of innocence is not analysed in relation to the outcome of the proceedings but rather in relation to the duration of the proceedings. As already indicated above, it is the length of the pre-trial detention proceedings, whatever the outcome of the trial, that is considered a punishment before the pronouncement of judgment.

The Respondent State cannot thus avail itself of the victim's acquittal to justify that the presumption of innocence, based on the prolonged duration of the victim's pre-trial detention, was not violated. On the contrary, if an acquittal occurs after a long period of pre-trial detention, the victim will have been punished despite his innocence; which would be contrary to the right to the presumption of innocence.

It follows that the right to the presumption of innocence as defined in Article 7(1)(b) has been violated. On the violation of the right to be tried within a reasonable time by an impartial court or tribunal

The Commission notes that the expression "reasonable time" comprises a juxtaposition of two terms: that of "time" and that of "reasonable". The first refers to an interval of time during which an action is accomplished; and in the context of judicial proceedings, an interval of time in which a judgment is delivered. As for the adjective "reasonable", it may be defined as what is logical and satisfactory. Thus, in the context of the African Charter, the expression "reasonable time" would mean an interval of time that is neither surprisingly long nor abusively short. In other words, the Charter requires that the trial be of an acceptable duration or one that is not excessively long.

So understood, it remains for the Commission to determine the length of a reasonable time. Neither the Charter nor other international human rights protection instruments give its exact and maximum length. However, in the case of Article 19 v. Eritrea, the Commission indicated that the question relating to what is reasonable cannot be expressed in terms of an overall time limit applicable to all cases, but must rather depend on the circumstances. It then referred to the European Court, which noted that these circumstances include the complexity of the case, the conduct of the trial and of the competent authorities

In this case, none of the three circumstances can justify a pre-trial detention period of 4 years which the complainant submits is not reasonable. The Commission does not share the view of the Respondent State, which considers this period reasonable in proceedings in which 21 accused were involved. Indeed, the involvement of 21 accused does not constitute a complexity capable of extending pre-trial detention to more than 4 years. The Commission also observes that the victim lodged an appeal in 2007 with the Administrative Court against the Minister of Posts and Telecommunications for payment of his salary arrears and damages linked to abusive prosecution, pain and suffering for unjustified imprisonment but that he had not yet received any follow-up in 2013, the date of the formulation of the Complainant's additional observations on the merits. The Respondent State gives no explanation for this although an opportunity to do so had been given to it.

In the case of Odjouoriby Cossi Paul v. Benin the Commission held that the fact that the appeal before the Court of Appeal was unduly prolonged is contrary to the spirit and the letter of the aforementioned Article 7(1)(d). Thus, the Commission considers that the time taken by the Cameroonian judicial authorities to decide on the violation of the Victim's rights, without demonstrating the circumstances which would have prevented the normal course of the trial, constitutes a violation of the right to a fair trial within the meaning of Article 7(1)(d) of the Charter. Observation of the Commission on the claims for reparation.

The Complainant alleges that he is entitled to reparation in respect of the alleged violations. The Commission notes that the African Charter does not contain a specific provision on reparation in the event of violation of the rights enshrined in it. However, in accordance with its jurisprudence, it notes that the violation of the rights protected by the Charter gives rise to a right to reparation. Thus, for example, in the communication Jean-Marie Atangana Mebara v. Republic of Cameroon, the Commission indicated that reparation may take various forms depending on the rights violated and the circumstances of the case, ranging from administrative, legislative and judicial actions to monetary compensation.

In this case, the complainant requests reparation in the form of monetary compensation of an overall value of 574,680,747 (Five Hundred and Seventy-Four million Six Hundred and Eighty Thousand Seven Hundred and Forty Seven CFA francs) which he divides into four categories: the victim's salary during the period of imprisonment; payment of interest of 6% per year for 13 years; damages for abusive prosecution, suffering and pain linked to his unjustified detention; and the costs associated with the various proceedings and refusal to pay. The Commission proposes to analyse them one by one. On the payment of the victim's salary arrears during the period of imprisonment

The Complainant first requests payment of his salary corresponding to the period from October 2000 to December 2003 which is equivalent to 13,865,592 CFA francs (Thirteen Million Eight Hundred and Sixty Five thousand five hundred and ninety-two CFA francs), that is, 38 months x 364,884 CFA francs. Having found violations of the Charter and, above all, a pre-trial detention that did not respect the principles established by the African Charter, the Commission indeed notes that the State responsible for these violations has the obligation to erase all the consequences of its acts and thus restore the victim to the situation in which he would have been had those acts not been committed.

It follows that the Commission consents to monetary reparation corresponding to the months in which the victim was not paid. It remains, however, to be seen whether the actual amount to be paid to him is equivalent to 13,865,592 CFA francs corresponding to arrears of 38 months as claimed by the Complainant, that is, 364,884 CFA francs per month. This is important because the principle is that reparation must be just, adequate, effective, sufficient, appropriate, victim-oriented and proportionate to the prejudice suffered.
